It started after moving house. My Nani sent her special oil and said, "Rub this every night and it will go." And I believed her. It did feel good. The warmth, her voice on the phone. I really think it helped me relax.
But after a few weeks it was still sharp when I bent down. So I kept the oil, and I also went to a doctor. I told her straight: "I'm hopeful, I'm using my Nani's oil, but I'm also scared I've damaged something." She examined me, sent me for a scan to be safe, and explained what was likely.
Turned out to be a strain. Physio now. Still using the oil.

qa.q: What did Asif's Nani send for the back pain?
qa.a: Asif's Nani sent her special oil.

qa.q: Why did Asif decide to see a doctor despite believing in the oil?
qa.a: Asif felt hopeful about the oil but also scared of having damaged something, because the pain was still sharp after a few weeks.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the oil for comfort while seeing a doctor worked, because it used hope without letting it replace a proper check.

qa.q: If you were Asif's Nani, how might you feel hearing the whole story?
qa.a: Nani might feel pleased that her oil still helped and relieved that Asif also saw a doctor and got the right treatment.

grounding: An adult welcomes comfort from a grandmother's remedy but sees a doctor for lasting back pain and shares worries openly.

passage:
In the kindergarten room, Miss Arohi crouched by Vandana's table. "You're such a bright girl. Show me how you'd sort these shells?"
Vandana sorted them into big and small. Miss Arohi smiled wide. "Clever! What else could we do?"
Miss Arohi stayed. She waited while Vandana thought. She asked another question, then another.
Vandana sat up tall. She sorted them by colour, then by shape. When the bell went, she was still trying a fourth way. At home she sorted Nani's buttons too.

qa.q: How did Vandana first sort the shells?
qa.a: She sorted them into big and small.

qa.q: Why did Vandana sit up tall and keep trying new ways?
qa.a: She felt proud and encouraged, because Miss Arohi called her bright and stayed with her, making trying feel worthwhile.

qa.q: How could Miss Arohi give every child this same boost?
qa.a: She could crouch down, wait and ask follow-up questions with every child, not only those she thinks are bright.

qa.q: What might another child at the table feel, watching Miss Arohi stay with Vandana?
qa.a: Another child might feel left out or less important, wishing for the same smiles and questions.

grounding: A young child whom the teacher calls bright receives more time and smiles and starts acting bright.

Wednesday. Charu Ma'am asked Omkar first when she held up the counting cards. She waited while he counted. She smiled when he got it. Omkar raised his hand three more times.
Friday. The new puzzle had lots of pieces. Other children gave up. Omkar kept turning each piece. "I'm bright," he told his friend. "I can do it." He did, almost. Charu Ma'am clapped anyway.

qa.q: How might Omkar's friend feel hearing him say "I'm bright"?
qa.a: The friend might feel impressed or a bit unsure, wondering whether they are bright too.

Rain hammered the tin roof of the preschool, and the room was loud and crowded because nobody could go outside. Kiran Miss sat with Pankaj anyway. "You're my bright boy. Can you build a tower as tall as your knee?"
Pankaj built one. It fell. Kiran Miss smiled. "Bright boys try again. I'll wait."
Other children shouted. Pankaj didn't look up. He built wider at the bottom this time. Kiran Miss kept smiling.
The tower reached his knee. Pankaj grinned and said, "Now as tall as my tummy!"

qa.q: How tall did Kiran Miss ask Pankaj to build the tower?
qa.a: She asked him to build a tower as tall as his knee.

qa.q: What does Pankaj's grin and new challenge suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: He feels proud and confident, because Kiran Miss's smiles and waiting made trying feel worth it.

qa.q: What small step helped Pankaj keep going after the tower fell?
qa.a: Kiran Miss saying she would wait and smiling helped him try again with a wider base.

qa.q: What would change if Kiran Miss had walked away when the tower fell?
qa.a: Pankaj might have given up in the noisy room, feeling that trying again did not matter.

grounding: A young child the teacher calls bright receives patient attention even in a noisy room and begins to act bright.

subtype: Labelled weak and living down to it [Receiver]
passage:
In Class 5, Jaya Ma'am had once said, "Mridul is weak at maths, let's not put him on the spot." Since then, maths class felt different.
When Jaya Ma'am asked a question, she looked at the front row. If Mridul raised his hand, she waited one second, then called on someone else. When he got a sum wrong, she said, "It's okay, beta," and moved on quickly, without asking him how he did it.
By December, Mridul had stopped raising his hand. He copied the answers from the board. In the test he left three questions blank.
"I'm just weak at maths," he told his mother. He said it the way he'd say his name.

qa.q: How many questions did Mridul leave blank in the test?
qa.a: He left three questions blank.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when he said "I'm just weak at maths"?
qa.a: He felt resigned and discouraged, believing the label as a fact about himself.

qa.q: How could Jaya Ma'am change the small cues she sends?
qa.a: She could wait longer after asking Mridul, call on him sometimes, and ask him to explain his steps when he gets something wrong.

qa.q: How might Mridul's mother feel hearing him say it like his name?
qa.a: His mother might feel worried and sad, seeing that a label has become part of how he sees himself.

grounding: A child labelled weak at maths gets less waiting time and fewer questions, stops raising his hand and comes to believe the label.

subtype: Labelled weak and living down to it [Receiver]
passage:
Tuesday. At tuition, Santosh Sir said to Indu's mother, "She's a bit weak in maths. We'll go slow." Indu heard it from the doorway.
The next Tuesday. Santosh Sir gave the others the harder worksheet. Indu got the easy one. When she put her hand up, he said, "Let's see if someone else knows," without waiting. She put her hand down.
Two weeks later. Indu no longer brought questions. She sat at the back and drew in her margin. When her mother asked about tuition, Indu shrugged. "I'm the weak one. Everyone knows."
She didn't try the bonus question on the class test. Why would she?

qa.q: What did Santosh Sir say to Indu's mother on the first Tuesday?
qa.a: He said, "She's a bit weak in maths. We'll go slow."

qa.q: What was Indu feeling when she said "I'm the weak one. Everyone knows"?
qa.a: She felt defeated and a little ashamed, having taken the label as the truth about herself.

qa.q: What could Indu's mother do after hearing that shrug?
qa.a: She could talk to Indu about the tuition, ask Santosh Sir to give Indu the harder worksheet and time to answer, and praise her effort at home.

qa.q: How might Santosh Sir see Indu's silence at the back?
qa.a: He might think she is simply weak and quiet, not noticing that his own small choices taught her to stop trying.

grounding: Over weeks, a girl labelled weak at maths gets easier sheets and less waiting time, stops asking questions and lives down to the label.

subtype: Labelled weak and living down to it [Receiver]
passage:
Zubin, beta, come, sit by me. You want to know why your Dadi still counts on her fingers? Let me tell you.
When I was nine, our maths teacher told my class, "Reena is weak at maths." Just once. But after that, he never waited for my answer. He would look at me, and then look away. He asked the other girls to the board, not me.
At first I kept raising my hand. Then I stopped. What was the use? By the end of the year, I believed it. I was weak. I even started making silly mistakes on sums I knew.
It took me thirty years and running my own shop to discover I could add perfectly well. That teacher's look, that little turning away, it taught me more than any lesson did.

qa.q: How old was Reena when her teacher called her weak at maths?
qa.a: She was nine.

qa.q: What was young Reena feeling when she stopped raising her hand?
qa.a: She felt hopeless and small, thinking there was no use because the teacher always looked away.

qa.q: What choice inside the story could the teacher have made differently?
qa.a: The teacher could have waited for her answer and called her to the board like the others, instead of looking away after labelling her.

qa.q: How might the other girls in the class have seen young Reena?
qa.a: They might have started to see her as the weak one too, since the teacher never asked her to the board.

grounding: A girl labelled weak at maths receives less waiting time and fewer chances, stops raising her hand and comes to believe the label.

subtype: Family verdict about who they will become [Receiver]
passage:
"Zainab got 96 again," said Phuppo, passing the plate of kebabs. "Salma, you'll never be like your cousin. Some children are just made for books."
Salma looked at her plate. "I know."
"Don't say 'I know,'" Ammi said quietly, after the guests had left. "Why did you say that?"
"Because it's true. Everyone says it. I'm the one who's not like Zainab."
"Salma, you went from 61 to 74 in science this year. That's not 'not like Zainab.' That's you working."
"It's still not 96."
"I don't need 96. I need you to keep doing what you did this year. I've watched you do it. I believe in that."
Salma was quiet. Then: "Can you help me with the chemistry chapter tomorrow?"
"After breakfast," Ammi said.

qa.q: What mark did Salma get in science this year?
qa.a: Salma went from 61 to 74 in science this year.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling when she said "I know" at dinner?
qa.a: She felt small and resigned, having started to accept Phuppo's verdict as part of who she is.

qa.q: Which choice by Ammi worked, and why?
qa.a: Ammi pointed to Salma's real progress and said she believed in her effort, which quietly lifted Salma enough to ask for help.

qa.q: How might Zainab feel if she heard Phuppo's comment?
qa.a: Zainab might feel awkward or uncomfortable, being used to make her cousin feel small.

grounding: A teenager who keeps hearing she will never be like her cousin starts to believe it, until her mother's steady belief in effort lifts her.

passage:
For years at family weddings someone would say it: "Avni, you'll never be like Rukmini." Rukmini was my cousin who got into the science college, sang at every function and never had a hair out of place.
I laughed along. By fourteen I had stopped entering the school singing competition. I told my friends I was "the average cousin." It was almost a joke, except I believed it. When a teacher suggested I try for the science olympiad, I said, "That's for people like Rukmini."
What changed it wasn't a big speech. It was Papa, every night that winter, asking, "What did you try today?" Not what marks, what I tried. Slowly I started having answers. I entered the olympiad. I didn't win. But I stopped saying "average cousin."

qa.q: What did Avni call themself in front of friends?
qa.a: Avni said "the average cousin."

qa.q: What was Avni feeling when saying the olympiad was for people like Rukmini?
qa.a: Avni felt small and discouraged, having turned the family comparison into a belief about who Avni could be.

qa.q: What could other parents learn from Papa's question?
qa.a: Asking "What did you try today?" every day shows steady belief in effort, which can quietly lift a child who has been labelled.

qa.q: How might Rukmini have felt hearing the comparison at every wedding?
qa.a: Rukmini may have felt uncomfortable or pressured, used as the measure for Avni.

grounding: A teenager repeatedly compared with a cousin adopts the verdict as identity, until a parent's nightly interest in effort lifts that belief.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Monday. From Disha, counsellor, Class 9 wing.
Pankaj came in because his class teacher noticed he had stopped submitting projects. When I asked why, he said, "There's no point. At home they say I'll never be like my cousin Yuvraj. He's at an engineering college. I'm the family failure."
He said it flatly, as if it were his name. He added that his father used to say it as a joke, and now Pankaj says it himself before anyone else can.
I asked what he'd enjoyed recently. He mentioned fixing his neighbour's cycle gears.
What I did next: I called his mother, with his permission, and shared how often he repeats this line. She was upset; she hadn't realised. We agreed she would notice and name his effort each week. Follow-up booked for Friday.

qa.q: What had Pankaj recently enjoyed fixing?
qa.a: He mentioned fixing his neighbour's cycle gears.

qa.q: Why does Pankaj say the line himself before anyone else can?
qa.a: He feels hurt and ashamed, and saying it first protects him from hearing it from others, though it also makes it his identity.

qa.q: What might help Pankaj start seeing himself differently?
qa.a: His mother noticing and naming his effort each week, and adults valuing skills like fixing gears, could steadily lift his view of himself.

qa.q: How might Pankaj's mother feel after the counsellor's call?
qa.a: She may feel upset and a little guilty, realising how deeply the family comparison had sunk in, and keen to help.

grounding: A teenager who hears he will never be like his cousin adopts it as identity, and a counsellor involves his mother to affirm his effort.
